messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Six months ago, during a late-night assignment covering a neighborhood protest, Elijah Vance found himself pinned against a patrol car. The air split with sirens. Heavy boots crunched on wet asphalt, closing in from both sides. Through the rolling window, the muffled bass of a specific pop track thumped from a passing cruiser. Officers moved with tactical precision, their hands resting heavily on their holsters. The moment stretched, suffocating. He remembered the exact cadence of their steps, the chilling chorus drifting across the asphalt, and the absolute certainty that the situation would only escalate. The way those sensory details fused that night now dictates his reality. Hearing a similar chord progression on the radio or hearing boots scuff against concrete outside his apartment instantly pulls him back into that car, the memory flooding his senses with the same visceral immediacy as the day it happened. As the recollections sharpen, his body prepares for imminent danger. He stops reading his drafts mid-sentence, his eyes darting to the door because focusing feels impossible when the threat feels so close. That hypervigilant scanning only feeds the mental replay. Every time he scans the room for exits, he catches fragments of the arrest: the glare of the headlights, the shouted commands, and he tries to reconstruct the sequence, but the narrative fractures before he can finish an account. The fragmented, overwhelming nature of these recollections convinces him that his mind is fundamentally broken. He sits alone in the dark, convinced his life has been irreparably dismantled, mourning the journalist who used to find joy in every assignment. Believing his life is ruined, he stops trying to make sense of the past, letting the vivid, unexplained flashbacks dominate his thoughts instead of confronting them. He begins to associate any sudden noise with that night, jumping at dropped files or distant car alarms, which only sharpens his sensitivity to the original cues. The constant alertness keeps his nervous system locked in overdrive. He avoids taking the subway or walking through unfamiliar neighborhoods because the layout offers no clear escape routes, and he can never properly assess the risk. When he is forced into open spaces, his eyes constantly sweep behind him, tracking every passerby for signs of pursuit, though this scanning only lasts a moment before he turns away. When the flashbacks or environmental cues hit, he retreats into rigid routines. He layers up in dark, oversized jackets even in spring, believing thick fabric will keep him from drawing attention. This isolation paradoxically amplifies the internal alarms. By shutting out the world to stay safe, he starves his brain of corrective experiences, leaving him hypersensitive to the slightest auditory or situational match. The exhaustion of constant defense convinces him he is no longer capable of doing the work that once defined him. He watches colleagues pack the newsroom with eager steps, feeling hollow and useless. Accepting that he is broken, he withdraws further. He stops listening to music entirely and avoids places where his girlfriend might remind him of the person he lost, ensuring he never has to process the grief of the aftermath. He also refuses to engage in any activity that might spark emotion, clinging to a numb baseline. The isolation confirms his worst fears. He sits in his dim apartment, telling himself he is miserable and that his career is over, while his girlfriend’s concerned messages go unanswered. This belief that his world is hostile fuels his paranoia. He becomes convinced that danger is always one misplaced step away, and the threat level in his mind never dips. The perceived danger dictates his daily armor. He wears concealing clothing to vanish into crowds and avoids anything that could spark feeling, treating his own emotional landscape like a minefield. His avoidance behaviors only reinforce the sense of vulnerability. By never testing the ground, he remains perpetually unsure of the danger, so he keeps looking behind him, assuming he is being followed. The chronic state of alarm convinces him that happiness is gone. He measures his days in skipped deadlines and missed dates, certain that his life has been destroyed. The conviction that he is ruined makes him hyperattentive to cues that prove his theory. When he hears footsteps or a certain song, he doesn't just flinch; he braces, interpreting them as confirmation of his helplessness. After six months of mounting silence, skipped deadlines, and his girlfriend’s growing worry, Elijah finally scheduled an intake. He walked into the clinic not because he believed he could fix himself, but because the loop of fear had finally outpaced his ability to endure it. He wanted to know if the journalist he used to be could ever return, or if the memories would always keep him pinned.
